N.b. if you are writing a version of forward_list yourself, do not use a namespace named __fl_detail. It is undefined behavior to define any names with __ at the front, those names are reserved for the implementation. Q: Our PHP backend is very slow because of the database connection A:

It could be anything, among others:

1. Network lag due to distance

Your application runs on machine1 and the database is hosted on machine2 and the request gets through the internet.

If you can host the database and the application on the same machine this is ameliorated or at least at the same physical location and internal network.

2. Underperforming firewall or router/network settings

If there are lots of rules to check by the router, then it can slow down requests.

3. Damaged hardware

Test your database server individually, see whether it's underperforming or not. There could be that something is damaged or there is a logical problem such as full disk.

4. Overload

If your database server is busy handling too many requests, then it will be slow to respond even if otherwise it would be quick to answer if the traffic was less.

5. Erroneous logic

Even though you use Doctrine, it's open-source, the connect function may have an underperforming overload.

In order to figure out what the exact problem is, test all the above separately, for example pinging the server that hosts the RDBMS server would test network reach overhead and if that's slow, then you have your answer. If that's not slow, you excluded a candidate problem.

Q: How to best organise python dependencies for Linux /usr/local/bin scripts A:

all packed in an .rpm

Rpms are installed by the system, so I would use /usr/bin and /usr directories.

/usr/local/* are for manual modifications, i.e. not rpm modifications.

If you want to have a nice place for your stuff without affecting the system, put your stuff from rpm in /opt/kmalarski_or_km_or_something_like_that/<package_name>/ .

is it a good practice to do it like this?

This is your system, there is no good practice. Do what works. Todays good practice is to use containers. You can also use uvx to just install and run your project ad-hoc.

I initially decided to install an extra file (say, /usr/local/bin/deps.py) with the shared code.

That is highly confusing. If deps.py is no an executable, why is it in bin? To install python dependencies, use python convention. See python rpm packaging guides https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/9/html/installing_and_using_dynamic_programming_languages/assembly_packaging-python-3-rpms_installing-and-using-dynamic-programming-languages . Python libraries should be put in %{python3_sitelib} or /usr/lib/python3.9/site-packages properly packaged with python.

If you do not want or do not have time or any other reason to properly care about packaging python application, then just consider putting your stuff in to /opt with whatever convention you desire.

Q: What is the difference between transaction isolation levels and optimistic/pessimistic concurrency control? A:

This is one of those topics where the terminology can get really blurry because they both deal with "concurrency," but they operate at different layers. To keep it simple: Isolation Levels are a database-level contract, while Optimistic/Pessimistic Locking are strategies you (the developer) choose to handle specific data integrity scenarios.

1. Isolation Levels (The "Environment" Rules)

Think of Isolation Levels as the "default behavior" of your database. When you set an isolation level (like READ_COMMITTED or REPEATABLE_READ), you are telling the DB engine: "How much do I want to see what others are doing right now?" It’s a global setting for the transaction. The DB uses its internal mechanisms (locks or MVCC) to prevent things like Dirty Reads or Phantom Reads. You don’t usually "code" these; you configure them.

2. Pessimistic vs. Optimistic (The "Strategy" Choice)

These are specific tactics you use for a particular piece of data.

• Pessimistic Locking: You assume the worst. You say, "I’m taking this row, and I don't want anyone else to even touch it until I’m done." It’s like a physical lock on a door. It relies heavily on the DB's internal locking

• Optimistic Locking: You assume everything will be fine. You don't lock the row. Instead, you keep a version number. If someone else updates it while you were working, the DB (or JPA) throws an error when you try to save. This isn't really a DB "lock" in the traditional sense; it's a version check.

Are they independent?

Yes and No. They are complementary.

• You can have a READ_COMMITTED isolation level and still use Optimistic Locking in your Java code to prevent "Lost Updates."

• Actually, in modern web apps, we rarely use the highest isolation level (SERIALIZABLE) because it kills performance. Instead, we use a lower level (like READ_COMMITTED) and handle specific conflicts using Optimistic Locking.
